stem: You reach a 45-year-old man sitting on a park bench holding his chest. He is alert and watching you approach. What should you do first?
options: Introduce yourself and ask if you may help him
Ask bystanders for his medical history first
Place a nonrebreather mask on him at 15 L/min
Begin a head-to-toe exam while he describes his pain
explanation: An alert adult must give expressed consent, and introducing yourself builds the rapport that makes the rest of the assessment work. Applying a mask or touching him without consent is unsafe for rapport and can be battery.

stem: While suctioning thick secretions from the airway of an unresponsive 4-year-old boy, what is the maximum duration of each suction attempt?
options: 5 seconds
10 seconds
15 seconds
Until the airway is fully clear
explanation: Children are suctioned no more than 10 seconds at a time (adults 15, infants 5) because suction removes oxygen along with secretions. Fifteen seconds is the adult limit and risks hypoxia and bradycardia in a child.

stem: Dispatch sends you to a bar for a 24-year-old man with a gunshot wound; police are en route but not on scene. You should:
options: Enter quickly since the shooter has probably fled
Park at the front door with lights off
Ask the caller by phone whether the scene is safe now
Stage nearby until police report the scene secure
explanation: At a violent scene the EMT stages at a safe distance until law enforcement secures it, because injured or dead rescuers help no one. A caller's opinion or an assumption that the shooter left is not a secured scene.

stem: A 62-year-old woman who speaks only Vietnamese has abdominal pain. Her 10-year-old grandson offers to translate. The best approach is to:
options: Speak English loudly and slowly to her
Request a trained interpreter or language line
Skip the history and transport without questions
Rely on the grandson for all medical questions
explanation: A trained interpreter gives accurate, private communication, while a child may omit or misread sensitive details. Use the grandson only for urgent basics when nothing better exists.

stem: A D cylinder reads 2,000 psi. You give 15 L/min by nonrebreather. Using a 200 psi safe residual, how long will it last?
options: About 21 minutes
About 19 minutes
About 34 minutes
About 10 minutes
explanation: Duration = (2,000 - 200) x 0.16 / 15 = 288 / 15, about 19 minutes. Skipping the 200 psi safe residual gives 21 minutes, and using the E constant of 0.28 gives about 34.

stem: A 45-year-old woman twisted her ankle stepping off a curb. She is alert with no other complaints. Your physical exam should be:
options: A focused exam of the injured ankle
A rapid head-to-toe trauma exam
A detailed exam deferred to the hospital
Vital signs only, with no hands-on exam
explanation: With an isolated injury and no significant mechanism, a focused exam of the complaint area is appropriate. A rapid full-body trauma exam is reserved for significant mechanisms or unresponsive patients.

stem: A 4-year-old girl with a painful, deformed forearm clings to her mother and cries as you approach. To assess her, you should:
options: Separate her from her mother to reduce distraction
Promise her that nothing you do will hurt
Examine her while she sits on her mother's lap
Start at her head and move quickly down
explanation: Keeping a young child with the caregiver lowers fear and improves cooperation, and toddlers tolerate a toe-to-head approach better. Promising no pain is dishonest and destroys trust when it does hurt.

stem: A 34-year-old woman is postictal after a seizure with snoring respirations. She gags as you insert an oropharyngeal airway. You should:
options: Advance it past the gag reflex and tape it in
Insert a smaller OPA without rotating it
Leave it partly inserted to hold the tongue forward
Remove it and insert a lubricated NPA
explanation: An OPA is only for patients with no gag reflex, and forcing one invites vomiting and aspiration. A lubricated nasopharyngeal airway, bevel toward the septum, is tolerated by patients who still gag.

stem: While en route, which dispatch details should prompt an early request for more resources? Select all that apply.
options: Roofer fell 25 feet onto concrete
Driver pinned with fuel leaking
Rollover with five occupants hurt
Adult with a twisted ankle
Teen with a steady nosebleed
explanation: A high fall suggests multisystem trauma that needs ALS, entrapment with a fuel leak needs the fire department, and five patients outnumber one crew. A twisted ankle or a nosebleed in a stable patient is handled by the responding unit.

stem: A 30-year-old man is pacing and shouting at a bus stop. Police have secured the scene. He yells that he does not want help. You should:
options: Restrain him on the cot before trying to talk with him
Ignore what he says and start your exam
Stand close and firmly order him to sit
Speak calmly, keep a safe distance, and listen
explanation: A calm voice, a safe distance and active listening de-escalate an agitated patient and protect the crew. Crowding or restraining him without need escalates the situation and restraint requires enough personnel and protocol.

stem: You enter a room and see a 58-year-old woman slumped in a chair, gray in color, with gurgling respirations. Your next action should be to:
options: Open and suction her airway immediately
Measure her blood pressure and pulse rate
Obtain a SAMPLE history from her husband
Ask her husband when she was last well
explanation: Gray skin and gurgling seen from the doorway mean she is sick and the airway is threatened, so it is managed at once. History and vital signs come after life threats to the airway are fixed.

stem: A 27-year-old man fell 15 feet, responds to pain, and has clear fluid draining from his nose and bruising behind both ears. Which adjunct should you avoid?
options: Oropharyngeal airway
Rigid-tip suction catheter
Nasopharyngeal airway
Bag-valve mask with oxygen reservoir
explanation: CSF from the nose and Battle's sign suggest a basilar skull fracture, where an NPA can pass through the fractured skull base. An OPA remains acceptable if he has no gag reflex, and suction and BVM are still needed.

stem: An E cylinder reads 1,200 psi. A COPD patient is on a nasal cannula at 4 L/min. How long will it last?
options: About 84 minutes
About 40 minutes
About 7 minutes
About 70 minutes
explanation: Duration = (1,200 - 200) x 0.28 / 4 = 280 / 4 = 70 minutes. Forgetting the 200 psi safe residual gives 84 minutes, and using the D constant of 0.16 gives 40.

stem: For each scene, specify whether the crew may approach the patient now or must stay back.
rows: Downed wire lying across the car
Large dog loose in the yard
explanation: A scene secured by police and a car stabilized by firefighters can be entered. Treat a downed wire as energized until the utility cuts power, stay upwind of an unknown vapor, and wait for a loose dog to be confined.

stem: The three components of the pediatric assessment triangle are:
options: Pulse, blood pressure, and respiratory rate
Appearance, work of breathing, circulation to skin
Airway, breathing, and circulation
Eye opening, best verbal response, and best motor response
explanation: The pediatric assessment triangle is a hands-off, across-the-room look at appearance, work of breathing and skin circulation. Airway, breathing, circulation is the hands-on primary survey that follows, and eye, verbal, motor is the GCS.

stem: A 2-year-old is ill. For each finding, specify which part of the pediatric assessment triangle it belongs to.
explanation: Gaze and tone are appearance, flaring and retractions are work of breathing, and mottling and pallor are circulation to skin. Pale lips may tempt a breathing answer, but the triangle scores skin color under circulation.

stem: You and your partner are ventilating a 58-year-old man who has a carotid pulse but is apneic. Which BVM approach is best?
options: One rescuer, one breath every 3 seconds
Two rescuers, one breath every 3 seconds
One rescuer, one breath every 8 to 10 seconds
Two rescuers, one breath every 6 seconds
explanation: An apneic adult with a pulse gets 1 breath every 6 seconds (10 per minute), each over 1 second with visible chest rise, and two-rescuer BVM gives the best mask seal. Every 3 seconds is the pediatric rate and overventilates an adult, causing gastric inflation and reduced venous return.

stem: A 28-year-old unrestrained driver hit a tree at 50 mph and responds only to pain. After the primary assessment, you should perform:
options: A focused exam of his chief complaint
An exam limited to the head and neck
A rapid full-body exam for hidden injuries
A detailed OPQRST interview with the patient
explanation: A significant mechanism with altered mental status calls for a rapid head-to-toe exam to find hidden life threats. A focused exam or OPQRST interview is not possible or adequate for a patient who responds only to pain.

stem: A 34-year-old woman lies very still on her side with her knees drawn to her chest and refuses to move. This position most suggests:
options: Respiratory distress from a lung infection such as pneumonia
Low blood sugar with confusion
The recovery phase after a seizure
Abdominal pain, possibly peritoneal irritation
explanation: Patients with peritoneal irritation lie still with knees drawn up because movement worsens the pain. A patient in respiratory distress usually sits upright or tripods rather than curling on the side.

stem: At night during an ice storm, you are sent to a rural farmhouse with a long unpaved driveway for a 70-year-old woman who fell. Before arrival you should:
options: Drive faster to make up for weather delays
Plan for access and icy footing hazards
Assume a private home is a safe scene
Leave equipment in the truck to move faster
explanation: Weather and access shape the plan: route, where to park, how to carry the patient over ice, and whether more hands are needed. Speeding on ice increases the risk of an ambulance crash, and no residence should be assumed safe.

stem: A 3-year-old girl pulled from a backyard pool has a pulse of 96 and gasping respirations of 4 per minute. How often should you ventilate her?
options: One breath every 6 seconds
One breath every 8 to 10 seconds
One breath every 2 to 3 seconds
Two quick breaths every 5 seconds
explanation: Children and infants with a pulse but inadequate breathing are ventilated at 1 breath every 2-3 seconds (20-30 per minute). Every 6 seconds is the adult rate and would underventilate this child; gasping is not adequate breathing.

stem: A 25-year-old man stabbed in the thigh is talking to you. Bright red blood is spurting and pooling under him. Your first action is to:
options: Control the bleeding immediately
Open his airway with a jaw thrust
Apply oxygen by nonrebreather mask
Count his respirations and radial pulse
explanation: Massive external bleeding is an obvious life threat that can kill in minutes, so it is controlled first. He is talking, so his airway is open and does not need to be opened before the bleeding is stopped.

stem: At the start of your shift, the AED self-test indicator shows an error. You should:
options: Take it out of service and replace it
Leave it in service until shift ends
Use it only if no other AED is nearby
Wait for the next scheduled weekly check
explanation: Equipment that fails a start-of-shift check must be removed from service and replaced, then reported per agency policy. Keeping a faulty AED on the unit risks a failure during a cardiac arrest.

stem: A 72-year-old woman found in bed opens her eyes and moans only when you speak loudly to her. On the AVPU scale she is:
options: Alert
Responsive to verbal stimuli
Unresponsive
Responsive to painful stimuli
explanation: She responds to your voice, so she is V on AVPU even though the response is only a moan. She is not P, because pain was not needed to get a response.

stem: A snapped utility pole has left a wire lying across the hood of a crashed car. The 40-year-old driver is alert and talking. You should:
options: Help him step out onto the dry pavement
Tell him to stay inside and request the power company
Move the wire aside with a dry wooden branch
Approach wearing rubber boots and gloves to assess him
explanation: Treat every downed wire as energized: an alert occupant is safest inside the vehicle until the utility cuts power. Stepping out, moving the wire or relying on boots can create a path to ground and electrocute the patient or rescuer.

stem: A 62-year-old woman with a cough and fever is alert, breathing 18 per minute without distress, and has an SpO2 of 92%. Which oxygen delivery is most appropriate?
options: Nonrebreather mask at 15 L/min
Bag-valve mask at 15 L/min
Nasal cannula at 2 to 4 L/min
No oxygen because she is not short of breath
explanation: Oxygen is indicated when SpO2 is below 94% per most protocols, and a low-flow nasal cannula is enough to bring this comfortable, alert patient to 94% or higher. A nonrebreather is for severe hypoxia or shock, and a BVM is for inadequate breathing.

stem: A 19-year-old found after a party does not respond to your voice but groans and pulls away when you pinch his trapezius. This means:
options: U on AVPU, and he needs CPR now
A on AVPU, and he is simply drunk
P on AVPU; he may not protect his airway
V on AVPU, and his airway is fully protected
explanation: Responding only to a painful stimulus places him at P, and patients at P or U often cannot protect their own airway. He reacts to pain, so he is not U, and nothing suggests cardiac arrest.

stem: After a fall, a 40-year-old man opens his eyes only to pain, makes incomprehensible sounds, and withdraws from pain. His Glasgow Coma Scale score is:
explanation: Eye opening to pain is 2, incomprehensible sounds is 2, and withdrawal from pain is 4, so 2 + 2 + 4 = 8. A score of 7 would require abnormal flexion, which scores 3 for motor.

stem: Family found an 80-year-old woman unresponsive in bed, and no history is available. After the primary assessment, your exam should be:
options: A focused exam of the region family points to
A rapid full-body medical assessment
Deferred until her family returns
A stroke scale exam only
explanation: An unresponsive medical patient cannot tell you what hurts, so a rapid full-body medical assessment comes first, then vitals and history from bystanders. A focused exam requires a responsive patient who can localize a complaint.

stem: A sedan lies on its side after a rollover, and the 22-year-old driver is moaning inside. Before anyone reaches in, you should:
options: Rock the car gently to test whether it is stable
Climb onto the upper side to open the door
Pull her through the windshield right away
Have trained personnel stabilize the vehicle
explanation: An unstable vehicle can roll onto rescuers or worsen the patient's injuries, so cribbing and stabilization come before access. Climbing on or rocking the car is exactly the movement that causes it to shift.

stem: Several adults have moderate to severe respiratory distress. For each, specify whether CPAP is appropriate or contraindicated per local protocol.
rows: Absent breath sounds after chest trauma
explanation: CPAP suits alert patients who follow commands, protect the airway and have a systolic pressure above 90, such as CHF or COPD in distress. Altered mental status, suspected pneumothorax and vomiting are contraindications even with a good blood pressure.

stem: During your rig check, the solution in an epinephrine auto-injector window looks brown and cloudy. You should:
options: Keep it on the unit as a backup dose
Shake it until it looks clear
Remove it and restock a new one
Use it first on the next call
explanation: Discolored or cloudy epinephrine has degraded and must be removed and replaced. Keeping it as a backup risks giving an ineffective dose to a patient in anaphylaxis.

stem: A 28-year-old woman in a crash opens her eyes spontaneously, is confused about the date, and follows commands. Her Glasgow Coma Scale score is:
explanation: Spontaneous eye opening is 4, confused speech is 4, and obeying commands is 6, so 4 + 4 + 6 = 14. A score of 15 requires fully oriented speech, which she lacks.

stem: An 80-year-old woman has been confused for 2 days, with a fever and foul-smelling urine. Her daughter says she is normally sharp. You should conclude:
options: This is a psychiatric problem, not medical
New confusion may signal infection and is significant
She is probably just tired and dehydrated from poor sleep
Confusion like this is normal at her age
explanation: A sudden change in mental status in an older adult is often the main sign of infection or another serious illness. Never assume confusion is normal aging, especially when the family says it is new.

stem: A family of four reports headache and nausea; two are drowsy, and a furnace ran all night with the windows shut. Your first action is to:
options: Move everyone to fresh air and request the fire department
Check pulse oximetry to rule out a low oxygen level
Begin assessing the drowsiest child right there in the living room
Open a window and start oxygen inside the house
explanation: Multiple patients with the same complaints in a closed, heated home suggest carbon monoxide, so the first step is to get everyone, including you, out of the atmosphere. Pulse oximetry reads falsely normal with carbon monoxide and cannot rule it out.

stem: Your 49-year-old cardiac arrest patient cannot be ventilated adequately with a BVM despite repositioning and an OPA. Per local protocol, the next step is:
options: Insert a supraglottic airway if authorized
Perform endotracheal intubation yourself
Stop ventilations and continue compressions only
Switch to a nonrebreather mask at 15 L/min
explanation: Where protocol permits, EMTs may place a supraglottic airway when BVM ventilation fails, then give 1 breath every 6 seconds with continuous compressions. Endotracheal intubation is outside EMT scope, and a nonrebreather cannot ventilate an arrested patient.

stem: A 6-month-old lies limp in her crib and does not respond when her mother calls her. To check responsiveness, you should:
options: Pinch her trapezius muscle hard
Shake her firmly by the shoulders
Tap or flick the soles of her feet
Rub her sternum firmly with your knuckles
explanation: Tapping or flicking the soles of the feet is the standard gentle stimulus for an infant. Shaking an infant can cause brain injury, and adult pain stimuli are not appropriate.

stem: A 65-year-old man is supine after a witnessed seizure with no trauma. He has snoring respirations at 14 per minute. Your first action is to:
options: Begin BVM ventilations at 10 breaths per minute
Apply a nonrebreather mask at 15 L/min
Suction his mouth for 15 seconds
Open the airway with a head-tilt chin-lift
explanation: Snoring means the tongue is partly blocking the upper airway, which is fixed by repositioning. Oxygen through a partly blocked airway does little, and his rate of 14 does not by itself call for ventilation.

stem: Place the steps for starting oxygen by nonrebreather from a new portable cylinder in order.
options: Prefill the reservoir bag
Attach the regulator to the cylinder
Place the mask on the patient
Remove the seal; crack the valve
Set the flow to 15 L/min
Open the valve; read the pressure
explanation: Cracking the valve blows out debris before the regulator goes on; then open the tank, confirm the pressure, set the flow and prefill the bag so the first breath is oxygen. A mask placed before the reservoir fills leaves the patient breathing against an empty bag.

stem: A 40-year-old man unresponsive from alcohol intoxication has a patent airway, adequate respirations of 14 per minute, and no suspected trauma. How should you position him?
options: Recovery position on his side
Supine with legs raised 12 inches
Prone with the head turned to one side
Seated upright at 90 degrees
explanation: An unresponsive patient who is breathing adequately and has no suspected spinal injury goes in the recovery position so vomit and secretions drain from the mouth. Supine lets the tongue and vomitus block the airway, and prone prevents airway monitoring.

stem: At a working house fire, a woman says her 60-year-old husband is still inside a smoke-filled bedroom. You should:
options: Crawl in low under the smoke to find him
Enter quickly wearing an N95 mask and eye protection
Send a bystander who knows the floor plan
Tell firefighters and stay out of the structure
explanation: Entry into a burning, smoke-filled building requires turnout gear, SCBA and training, so the EMT relays the information to firefighters and prepares to treat. An N95 offers no protection against smoke, heat or carbon monoxide.

stem: A 58-year-old man with chest pain answers your questions. For each answer, specify the OPQRST element it addresses.
explanation: What he was doing when it began is onset, what makes it better or worse is provocation, the description is quality and spread to the jaw is radiation. Shoveling snow may tempt provocation, but it tells you when the pain started.

stem: An adult has noisy breathing. Which sounds point to a problem in the upper airway? Select all that apply.
options: Snoring on inspiration
Gurgling with each breath
High-pitched inspiratory stridor
Expiratory wheezing
Fine crackles at the bases
explanation: Snoring (the tongue), gurgling (fluid) and stridor (swelling or a foreign body) come from the upper airway and call for positioning, suction or rapid transport. Wheezing comes from narrowed lower airways and crackles from fluid in the alveoli.

stem: A feverish 3-year-old girl sits upright, drooling, with high-pitched inspiratory stridor. She is anxious but alert. You should:
options: Lay her supine and insert an oral airway to hold it open
Keep her calm with her parent and transport
Look at her throat with a tongue depressor
Give 5 back slaps and 5 chest thrusts
explanation: Drooling, fever and stridor suggest epiglottitis, and upsetting her or probing the throat can cause complete obstruction. Keep her in a position of comfort with her parent, give oxygen as tolerated, and transport.

stem: A 66-year-old man with a laryngectomy stoma in his neck is apneic but has a pulse. How should you deliver BVM ventilations?
options: Seal an adult mask over the mouth and nose
Seal an infant or child mask over the stoma
Insert an OPA and ventilate through the mouth
Cover the stoma and ventilate through the mouth
explanation: A laryngectomy patient breathes only through the stoma, so seal a small round mask over it and ventilate; close the mouth and nose if air escapes there. Ventilating through the mouth will not reach the lungs of a total laryngectomy patient.

stem: At a highway crash, a fire engine is parked behind the wreck blocking the lane. Where should the ambulance park?
options: Behind the engine, upstream of the crash
Beside the wreck in the open travel lane for quick loading
Beyond the crash, downstream from the wreckage
In the median across both directions
explanation: The larger apparatus blocks upstream to shield the scene, and the ambulance parks past the crash so the patient can be loaded behind protection. Parking in an open lane or the median exposes the crew to traffic.

stem: A 35-year-old man in a restaurant clutches his throat. He cannot speak or cough and his lips are turning blue. You should:
options: Give 2 rescue breaths, then reassess
Encourage him to keep coughing hard
Give back blows and abdominal thrusts
Perform a blind finger sweep
explanation: Inability to speak or cough means a severe obstruction, treated in a conscious adult with cycles of 5 back blows and 5 abdominal thrusts per current guidelines and local protocol. Coughing is only encouraged in a mild obstruction with good air exchange, and blind finger sweeps can push the object deeper.

stem: You wrote the wrong pulse rate on a paper PCR before submitting it. The correct way to fix the error is to:
options: Black it out and write over it
Cover it with correction fluid
Start a new PCR and discard the original one
Draw one line through it, initial and date
explanation: A single line through the error, with initials and date, keeps the original readable and shows the correction was honest. Obliterating the entry or discarding the original looks like falsification.

stem: A 22-year-old motorcyclist is unresponsive at a crash scene with snoring respirations. The best way to open his airway is the:
options: Tongue-jaw lift with neck extension
Head-tilt chin-lift maneuver
Head tilt with the neck fully hyperextended
Jaw-thrust maneuver without head tilt
explanation: A jaw thrust opens the airway while keeping the cervical spine in line for a patient with possible spinal injury. If the jaw thrust does not open the airway, the airway takes priority and a head tilt is then used.

stem: A 30-year-old man with a head injury has a GCS of 5, a fixed dilated left pupil, and extension posturing. How should you ventilate him?
options: About 10 breaths per minute regardless of signs
About 20 breaths per minute per protocol
About 30 breaths per minute to lower pressure
About 6 breaths per minute to avoid gastric distension
explanation: Hyperventilation is reserved for signs of brain herniation such as a unilateral fixed dilated pupil, posturing or Cushing's triad; an adult is then ventilated at about 20 per minute per protocol. Routine hyperventilation, or rates as high as 30, constricts cerebral vessels and worsens brain ischemia.

stem: You arrive for a 55-year-old diabetic man who is confused, but a large dog is lunging and barking at the screen door. You should:
options: Ask the occupant to secure the dog first
Enter slowly while keeping eye contact with the dog
Distract the dog with food and walk past
Use your jump bag as a shield and go in
explanation: Animals are a scene hazard; the crew does not enter until the dog is confined by the owner or animal control. A bitten EMT becomes a second patient and cannot care for the first.

stem: An unresponsive 50-year-old with no gag reflex needs an oropharyngeal airway. Place the insertion steps in order.
options: Insert with the tip toward the palate
Rest the flange on the lips
Measure mouth corner to earlobe
Rotate 180 degrees while advancing
Open the mouth with crossed fingers
explanation: Size the airway first, open the mouth, insert it tip up so it slides over the tongue, then rotate it into place until the flange rests on the lips. Rotating before the tip reaches the back of the tongue can push the tongue into the pharynx.

stem: A 62-year-old woman describes her abdominal pain as tearing and says it moves into her back. These answers describe:
options: Onset and time
Quality and radiation
Provocation and severity
Severity and time
explanation: Tearing describes the quality of the pain and moving into the back describes radiation, a pattern that should raise concern for an aortic aneurysm. Severity is the 1-10 rating, not the description.

stem: You begin CPR on a 55-year-old woman in cardiac arrest. What compression rate and depth should you use?
options: 80-100 per minute, 1.5 inches deep
120-140 per minute, 2.5 to 3 inches deep
100-120 per minute, 1.5 to 2 inches
100-120 per minute, 2 to 2.4 inches
explanation: AHA adult CPR is 100-120 compressions per minute at 2 to 2.4 inches with full chest recoil. Shallower compressions do not generate adequate blood flow, and rates above 120 shorten filling time.

stem: A 45-year-old man still snores after repositioning following a seizure. His teeth are clenched and he has a gag reflex. There is no head trauma. The best adjunct is:
options: An oropharyngeal airway
A lubricated nasopharyngeal airway
A supraglottic airway device
A bite block forced between the teeth
explanation: An NPA is tolerated by patients with a gag reflex and does not need the mouth opened. An OPA or supraglottic airway would trigger gagging and vomiting in a patient who still gags.

stem: A 30-year-old assaulted with a bat has bruising behind both ears and clear fluid draining from his nose. He has snoring respirations. Which is contraindicated?
options: A jaw-thrust maneuver
Suctioning blood from the mouth
A nasopharyngeal airway
Supplemental oxygen
explanation: Battle's sign and fluid from the nose point to a basilar skull fracture, so an NPA could enter the cranial vault. Jaw thrust, oral suction and oxygen are all appropriate.

stem: While you assess an intoxicated 28-year-old man, he suddenly pulls a knife and threatens your partner. You should:
options: Retreat to safety and call law enforcement
Disarm him while your partner holds his arms
Keep treating him while speaking in a calm voice
Secure him to the stretcher with soft restraints
explanation: A weapon makes the scene unsafe, so the crew withdraws and waits for police to secure it before resuming care. Disarming or restraining an armed person is a law enforcement task, not an EMT one.

stem: After submitting a PCR, you recall that the patient's daughter gave her aspirin before you arrived. You should:
options: Edit the original narrative to add it
Leave it out because your crew did not give it
Add a dated addendum marked as a late entry
Tell the nurse and skip documenting it
explanation: Information added after submission goes in a dated, labeled late entry or addendum, never by altering the original report. Pre-arrival medications are pertinent and must be documented.

stem: You and your partner perform CPR on a 6-month-old infant in cardiac arrest. Which technique and ratio are correct?
options: Two fingers on the lower sternum, 30:2
Two hands on the sternum, 15:2
Two-thumb encircling hands, 15:2
Two-thumb encircling hands, 30:2
explanation: With two rescuers, infants and children receive 15 compressions to 2 breaths, and the two-thumb encircling technique compresses about 1.5 inches, one third of chest depth. The 30:2 ratio is for a single rescuer, and two hands are for larger children and adults.

stem: A 40-year-old man rescued from a house fire has singed nasal hair, soot in his mouth, and a hoarse voice. He is alert. This means:
options: He needs only a nasal cannula at 2 L/min
Minor smoke irritation that is not urgent
He can wait for a full secondary exam on scene
His airway may swell shut; transport rapidly
explanation: Singed nasal hair, soot and hoarseness are signs of an airway burn, and swelling can close the airway quickly. He needs high-flow oxygen, ALS and rapid transport rather than delay on scene.

stem: You find a 48-year-old man slumped in a chair with no trauma. He moans when you speak. Place the primary assessment steps in order.
options: Assess breathing adequacy
Form a general impression
Decide transport priority
Open and assess the airway
Check pulse, skin and bleeding
Check responsiveness with AVPU
explanation: The general impression and AVPU come first, then airway, breathing and circulation in that order, ending with a transport decision. In a breathing medical patient without major bleeding, circulation does not come before the airway.

stem: While you treat a 19-year-old with a gunshot wound to the thigh in a park, a hostile crowd gathers and begins shouting. You should:
options: Finish a complete secondary assessment on scene
Ask the crowd to form a protective circle
Load him promptly and continue care en route
Leave him and wait inside the ambulance
explanation: When a crowd turns hostile, the safest choice is to move the patient into the ambulance and leave, treating life threats on the way. Staying for a full assessment prolongs the danger, and abandoning the patient is not appropriate while you can safely remove him.

stem: CPR is in progress on a 55-year-old woman when the AED arrives. Place the AED steps in order.
options: Clear everyone for analysis
Resume compressions right away
Apply pads to the bare chest
Press shock when advised
Turn on the AED
explanation: Power on, attach the pads, keep everyone clear while it analyzes, shock if advised, then resume compressions at once for 2 minutes. Pausing for a pulse check right after the shock instead of resuming CPR wastes perfusion time.

stem: A 5-year-old with asthma has respirations of 44, retractions, and speaks in short phrases. SpO2 is 91%. Her breathing is best described as:
options: Anxiety hyperventilation that needs coaching
Respiratory distress; the rate is too fast
Normal, since children breathe faster than adults
Apnea requiring immediate CPR
explanation: Normal respirations for a school-age child are about 20 to 30, so 44 with retractions and low SpO2 is distress. Children do breathe faster than adults, but not this fast.

stem: A 24-year-old man with diabetes is confused and sweaty. Asking when he last ate addresses which SAMPLE element?
options: Last oral intake
Pertinent past history
Events leading up
Signs and symptoms
explanation: The L in SAMPLE is last oral intake, which is key for suspected hypoglycemia. His diabetes is pertinent past history, but the question about his last meal is the L element.

stem: An alert, oriented 55-year-old with chest pain refuses transport. Which belong in your refusal documentation? Select all that apply.
options: His decision-making capacity
Risks explained, including death
His signature and a witness
Advice to call 911 again
Your opinion of his choice
That he was rude to the crew
explanation: A defensible refusal shows capacity, informed risks, a witnessed signature and advice to call back, with medical direction contacted per local protocol. Opinions and labels about his manner are not objective and weaken the record.

stem: A sleepy 4-month-old with bronchiolitis has shallow respirations of 12 per minute with pauses. Pulse is 90. You should:
options: Give blow-by oxygen and observe her closely en route
Apply a nasal cannula at 2 L/min
Ventilate with a BVM at 20-30 per minute
Start chest compressions at 15:2
explanation: An infant should breathe 30 to 60 times a minute, so 12 with pauses is inadequate and needs ventilation at 1 breath every 2 to 3 seconds. Her pulse is low but above 60, so ventilation, not compressions, comes first.

stem: A 35-year-old construction worker is buried to the waist in a partially collapsed trench and is calling for help. You should:
options: Climb in to give oxygen and reassurance
Lower your partner into the trench on a rope to assess him
Stay out and request a technical rescue team
Dig the soil from around him with shovels
explanation: Trench walls can collapse again without warning, so only trained rescuers using shoring enter; the EMT stays clear and calls for technical rescue. Entering or digging adds weight and vibration near the edge and creates more victims.

stem: A 45-year-old man rescued from icy water is pulseless and very cold to the touch. The AED advises a shock. You should:
options: Shock once, resume CPR, handle him gently
Withhold all shocks until he is rewarmed
Deliver three stacked shocks, then check a pulse
Rub his arms and legs vigorously before shocking
explanation: In severe hypothermia, deliver the indicated shock, immediately resume CPR, and handle the patient gently because rough movement can trigger VF; further shocks follow local protocol. Stacked shocks are no longer used, and rubbing the extremities is harmful.

stem: A 59-year-old man collapsed at work. He is unresponsive and makes occasional gasping breaths about every 15 seconds. These breaths should be treated as:
options: A normal post-fainting breathing pattern
Adequate breathing at a slow rate
Hyperventilation from anxiety
Agonal gasps, not effective breathing
explanation: Occasional gasps in an unresponsive patient are agonal respirations and are a sign of cardiac arrest. Mistaking them for breathing delays CPR and the AED.

stem: A 67-year-old woman with COPD sits in a tripod position, uses her neck muscles to breathe, speaks two words at a time, and has cyanotic lips. Respirations are 32. This indicates:
options: Severe respiratory distress
A normal pattern for a COPD patient
Anxiety with adequate breathing
Mild distress typical of stable COPD
explanation: Tripod position, accessory muscle use, two-word dyspnea and cyanosis are all signs of inadequate breathing. COPD patients may live with some breathlessness, but these findings are never their baseline.

stem: A 23-year-old has spurting thigh bleeding that soaks through firm direct pressure. Place the tourniquet steps in order.
options: Lock the windlass in its clip
Place it 2 to 3 inches above the wound
Record the time applied
Pull the strap tight and secure it
Twist the windlass until bleeding stops
explanation: The tourniquet goes above the wound and is snugged down first, then the windlass is turned until bleeding stops, locked, and the time recorded for the hospital. Twisting before the strap is snug wastes turns and may never close the artery.

stem: A 12-year-old has fallen through pond ice and clings to the edge about 30 feet out. You have no ice rescue training. You should:
options: Walk out on the ice to grab him
Swim out to him with a rope tied around your waist
Lie flat and crawl out to pull him
Reach or throw a flotation device from shore
explanation: Untrained rescuers follow reach, throw, row, go and stay ashore while specialized rescue is requested. Going onto the ice or into the water without training and equipment often adds a second victim.

stem: A 70-year-old man with heart failure has crackles in both lower lungs and an SpO2 of 88%. Crackles most likely indicate:
options: A partial upper airway obstruction
Fluid in the small airways and alveoli
Air trapped in the pleural space
Narrowed lower airways from bronchospasm
explanation: Crackles, or rales, are fine popping sounds caused by fluid in the small airways, typical of pulmonary edema in heart failure. Bronchospasm causes wheezing, and upper airway obstruction causes stridor.

stem: A 30-year-old man smells of alcohol and says he drank six beers. Which entry best belongs in your PCR narrative?
options: Patient is drunk and belligerent.
Patient states he drank "six beers" tonight.
Patient appears to be an alcoholic.
Patient is clearly intoxicated, per crew impression.
explanation: Objective documentation quotes the patient and records observations, which makes the PCR defensible. Labels like drunk or alcoholic are opinions and may be considered libel.

stem: A 40-year-old woman with hives gives this history. For each statement, specify the SAMPLE element it belongs to.
rows: "I was gardening when I got stung"
explanation: A known drug reaction is an allergy, current drugs are medications, lifelong asthma is past history, and what she was doing when it began is events. The sting may tempt allergies, but it is what happened today, so it belongs to events.

stem: A 30-year-old woman, 30 weeks pregnant with pneumonia, is alert with respirations of 22 and good chest rise. SpO2 is 91%. You should:
options: Begin BVM ventilations at 10 per minute
Withhold oxygen to avoid harming the developing fetus
Give oxygen; her ventilation is adequate
Insert an oral airway and assist breaths
explanation: She is alert with an adequate rate and depth but is hypoxic, so she needs oxygen, not assisted ventilation. Oxygen protects the fetus too, so withholding it is wrong.

stem: A 31-year-old woman has a stab wound to the right groin with steady dark bleeding that direct pressure is not controlling. The next step is:
options: Apply a tourniquet directly over the groin wound
Elevate the leg and place ice packs on it
Cover it with a dry dressing and transport
Pack it with hemostatic gauze and hold pressure
explanation: Junctional wounds of the groin or axilla cannot be controlled with a tourniquet, so pack the wound tightly with hemostatic or plain gauze, hold firm pressure, then secure a pressure dressing. Elevation, ice and a loose dressing do not control this bleeding.

stem: Your gloves are on. In which situations should you also wear eye protection? Select all that apply.
options: Arterial bleeding spurting from the arm
Suctioning vomit from an airway
Delivering a baby in the field
Taking a BP over intact skin
Applying a cold pack to an ankle
explanation: Arterial spray, suctioning and childbirth can all splash blood or fluid into the eyes, so eye protection is added to gloves. Taking a blood pressure or applying a cold pack over intact skin carries no splash risk.

stem: In which situations can a pulse oximetry reading be inaccurate? Select all that apply.
options: Suspected carbon monoxide poisoning
Cold fingers with poor perfusion
Dark nail polish on the finger
Shivering with a moving hand
Warm, still, well-perfused finger
Oxygen by nasal cannula
explanation: Carbon monoxide reads as oxygen and gives a falsely normal value, while cold fingers, dark polish and motion give low or erratic readings. Supplemental oxygen raises the true saturation but does not make the reading wrong.

stem: A 77-year-old woman with cold hands and dark nail polish has an SpO2 of 82% with an erratic waveform. She is pink and speaking full sentences. You should:
options: Move the probe to a warmer site without polish
Begin BVM ventilations immediately
Accept the reading and call for ALS
Stop using pulse oximetry on this call
explanation: Cold fingers and dark nail polish cause false low readings, and her clinical picture does not match the number. Treat the patient, not the monitor, and recheck at a better site such as another finger or the earlobe.

stem: A 38-year-old woman fell from a horse and has a tender, distended abdomen, pulse 124, BP 86/60, and cool clammy skin. Besides oxygen, you should:
options: Keep her supine and warm, transport rapidly
Give small sips of water for her thirst
Sit her upright for patient comfort
Stay on scene to obtain several sets of vital signs
explanation: Decompensated hypovolemic shock from likely internal bleeding needs oxygen, supine positioning, prevention of heat loss and rapid transport to surgical care, with ALS per protocol. Nothing is given by mouth, and delaying on scene worsens outcome.

stem: A 60-year-old woman with chest pain denies shortness of breath and nausea. Documenting these denials records:
options: Pertinent negatives
The chief complaint
Objective findings
The mechanism of injury
explanation: Pertinent negatives are findings you would expect but the patient denies, and they are a standard PCR element. They are reported by the patient, so they are not objective findings.

stem: A 50-year-old man recently released from prison has a productive cough, night sweats, weight loss, and is coughing up blood. You should wear:
options: A surgical mask only
Gloves and a gown only
Eye protection and gloves only
A fit-tested N95 respirator
explanation: These findings suggest tuberculosis, which spreads by the airborne route, so the EMT wears a fit-tested N95 and places a surgical mask on the patient if tolerated. A surgical mask on the EMT does not filter airborne particles.

stem: In an unresponsive infant, the preferred site to check for a pulse is the:
options: Carotid artery
Brachial artery
Dorsalis pedis artery
Radial artery
explanation: The brachial artery on the inside of the upper arm is the recommended pulse check site for infants. An infant's short, chubby neck makes the carotid pulse hard to find.

stem: A 45-year-old man is awake after a car crash. You cannot feel a radial pulse, but his carotid pulse is weak and rapid. This suggests:
options: Cardiac arrest requiring chest compressions
An isolated injury to his arm only
Poor perfusion, likely decompensated shock
A normal finding in an anxious patient
explanation: A missing radial pulse with a weak, fast carotid pulse means blood pressure is low enough to lose peripheral pulses. He has a carotid pulse, so this is shock, not cardiac arrest.

stem: A 58-year-old man has crushing chest pain radiating to his jaw. He has no aspirin allergy and no active bleeding. Per protocol, give aspirin:
options: 162-324 mg, chewed
81 mg, swallowed whole
650 mg, swallowed with water
324 mg, placed under the tongue
explanation: Chewing 162-324 mg of aspirin speeds absorption and inhibits platelet clumping in acute coronary syndrome. Aspirin is withheld for allergy or active bleeding, and it is not a sublingual medication.

stem: During a rapid trauma exam of a fall victim, the letter L in DCAP-BTLS stands for:
options: Lesions
Lividity
Lacerations
Level of consciousness
explanation: DCAP-BTLS is deformities, contusions, abrasions, punctures or penetrations, burns, tenderness, lacerations and swelling. Lividity is a sign of death, not part of the mnemonic.

stem: A 28-year-old woman, 34 weeks pregnant, fell down stairs. She is anxious, pale, cool, and clammy. Pulse is 118 and BP is 112/70. You should suspect:
options: A normal pregnancy-related heart rate
Anxiety only, since her BP is normal
Neurogenic shock from a spinal injury
Compensated shock that pregnancy can mask
explanation: Pale, cool, clammy skin with tachycardia and a normal BP is compensated shock, and the larger blood volume of pregnancy can hide significant blood loss. A normal BP does not rule out shock, and neurogenic shock causes warm, dry skin with a slow pulse.

stem: A 25-year-old woman is crowning, with heavy amniotic fluid and blood expected. Beyond gloves, which PPE should you add?
options: A second pair of gloves alone
An N95 respirator alone
Gown, mask, and eye protection
A helmet with a face shield and turnout coat
explanation: Childbirth produces large volumes of blood and fluid that can splash the face and soak clothing, so a gown, mask and eye protection are indicated. Double gloves or an N95 alone do not protect the eyes or clothing.

stem: A 57-year-old man with chest pain asks for help taking his nitroglycerin. Which findings mean you should withhold it? Select all that apply.
options: Systolic BP of 84
Tadalafil taken 30 hours ago
Prescription in his wife's name
Sildenafil taken 72 hours ago
Heart rate of 88
Pain that began an hour ago
explanation: Withhold nitroglycerin for a systolic pressure below 90 to 100 per local protocol, tadalafil within 48 hours, or a prescription that is not the patient's own. Sildenafil is restricted for 24 to 48 hours depending on protocol, so a dose 72 hours ago does not by itself rule it out.

stem: For each finding in a child after 2 days of vomiting, specify whether it is an early or a late sign of shock.
explanation: Tachycardia, delayed refill and restlessness are compensation, while hypotension, bradycardia and lethargy mean the child is decompensating. Children hold a normal blood pressure until late, so a falling pressure is never an early sign.

stem: For each patient, specify whether care proceeds under expressed or implied consent.
rows: Alert adult agrees to a splint
Alert woman holds out her arm for a BP
explanation: Agreement by words or by action, such as holding out an arm, is expressed consent. Implied consent covers an unresponsive or seizing adult and a minor who needs emergency care when no parent can be reached.

stem: A 19-year-old struck by a car lies supine in dark clothing on wet pavement. His airway is open and breathing is adequate. To check for major bleeding, you should:
options: Check his blood pressure, since bleeding lowers it early
Expose him and sweep gloved hands beneath him
Ask him whether he feels any bleeding
Wait for the secondary assessment to look
explanation: Dark clothing and wet pavement hide blood, so you expose and sweep under the patient during the primary assessment to find life-threatening bleeding. Hypotension is a late sign, so waiting for it misses the bleeding.

stem: You must stay with a 45-year-old trapped driver while firefighters cut the roof with hydraulic tools. Appropriate PPE includes:
options: Gloves, a surgical mask, and a disposable gown
An N95 respirator with gloves and shoe covers
A reflective vest with a single pair of gloves
Helmet, eye protection, and turnout gear
explanation: Extrication produces flying glass, sharp metal and debris, so anyone inside the vehicle needs a helmet, eye protection and turnout gear over medical gloves. A disposable gown or vest does not protect against cuts or impact.

stem: A 52-year-old man with hypertension has a steady nosebleed, is alert, and has a BP of 178/98. How should you control the bleeding?
options: Tilt his head back and pinch the soft nostrils
Lay him supine with ice on his neck
Pack both nostrils tightly with gauze
Have him lean forward; pinch the nostrils
explanation: Leaning forward while pinching the soft nostrils keeps blood out of the airway and stomach, where it can cause vomiting or aspiration. Tilting the head back sends blood down the throat.

stem: A 35-year-old has a chainsaw wound to the lower leg. Bright red blood keeps soaking through firm direct pressure. You should next:
options: Apply a tourniquet directly over the knee
Remove soaked dressings and apply fresh ones
Apply a tourniquet 2-3 inches above the wound
Elevate the leg and use pressure points
explanation: Life-threatening extremity bleeding that direct pressure cannot control needs a tourniquet placed 2 to 3 inches above the wound and not over a joint. Removing soaked dressings disrupts clots, and elevation with pressure points is not reliable.

stem: A 6-year-old pulled from a pool is unresponsive and apneic. You feel no pulse within 10 seconds. With two rescuers, you should begin:
options: CPR at 30 compressions to 2 breaths
Rescue breathing only at 20 per minute
Abdominal thrusts to clear the water
CPR at 15 compressions to 2 breaths
explanation: A child with no pulse needs CPR, and two-rescuer child CPR uses a 15:2 ratio to give more ventilations. Rescue breathing alone is for a child who has a pulse, and abdominal thrusts delay care and do not remove aspirated water.

stem: A 22-year-old assault victim has bruising behind both ears found during your head exam. This finding suggests:
options: A simple scalp contusion
A fractured mandible
A cervical spine fracture
A basilar skull fracture
explanation: Bruising over the mastoid process (Battle's sign) suggests a basilar skull fracture, which also means avoiding a nasopharyngeal airway. It is a late sign of a deep fracture, not a simple scalp bruise.

stem: A placarded tanker is leaking a vapor cloud, and its 40-year-old driver lies near the cab. Trained at awareness level, you should:
options: Wear an N95 and quickly drag him clear
Stay upwind in the cold zone and call HazMat
Hold your breath and pull him out
Approach from downhill wearing a gown and gloves
explanation: Awareness-level EMTs recognize the hazard, isolate, stay upwind and uphill in the cold zone, and request HazMat; patients are decontaminated before EMS treats them. No standard EMS PPE, including an N95, protects against an unknown chemical vapor.

stem: A 29-year-old driver, alert and sober, has midline neck tenderness after a rear-end crash. She is seated in her car with no deficits. You should:
options: Rapidly extricate her onto a long backboard with straps
Skip spinal precautions since she has no deficits
Have her walk to the ambulance without a collar
Apply a collar and let her self-extricate to the cot
explanation: Midline tenderness is an indication for spinal motion restriction, but an alert, cooperative patient moves the spine least by self-extricating to the cot with a collar on. Long backboards are for patients who cannot move themselves, and normal neurologic findings do not rule out injury.

stem: An on-duty EMT fails to splint an obvious fracture, and the patient suffers nerve damage. Negligence requires duty, breach, causation and:
options: Intent
Abandonment
Battery
Damages
explanation: Negligence requires a duty to act, a breach of that duty, damages and proof that the breach caused the damages. Intent is not required, and Good Samaritan laws do not protect on-duty EMTs.

stem: A 72-year-old woman has right facial droop, right arm drift and slurred speech. Her husband says she was normal at bedtime and woke this way. Her last known well time is:
options: When she woke with symptoms
When she went to bed
When her husband called 911
When you arrived on scene
explanation: Last known well is the last time the patient was seen at her neurologic baseline, so for a wake-up stroke it is when she went to bed. Using the time she woke would wrongly place her inside treatment windows that may have closed.

stem: A 58-year-old diabetic man reports 30 minutes of chest pressure radiating to his jaw, with sweating and nausea. BP 148/90, pulse 96, SpO2 95%. You should suspect:
options: Gastric reflux after a meal
Chest wall muscle strain
Acute coronary syndrome
A panic attack
explanation: Pressure radiating to the jaw with diaphoresis and nausea in a diabetic male is acute coronary syndrome until proven otherwise, which calls for aspirin, an early 12-lead where permitted and prompt transport. Reflux or anxiety are diagnoses of exclusion an EMT should never assume.

stem: During a long extrication, saws and a generator run continuously beside the vehicle. Which PPE is often overlooked?
options: A second pair of exam gloves
A fit-tested N95 respirator for airborne infection
Disposable shoe covers
Hearing protection for rescuers and the patient
explanation: Prolonged high noise from tools and generators can cause hearing damage and blocks communication, so hearing protection is part of extrication PPE for crews and the patient. Shoe covers and an extra pair of gloves do not address the noise hazard.

stem: A 25-year-old has a painful, deformed forearm with good distal pulses. Place the splinting steps in order.
options: Measure the splint on the uninjured arm
Apply manual stabilization
Recheck distal pulse, motor and sensation
Check distal pulse, motor and sensation
Secure joints above and below the injury
explanation: Stabilize the limb, document pulse, motor and sensation, size the splint and immobilize the joints above and below, then recheck function. Without the first check, a later loss of pulse cannot be tied to the splint.

stem: A 9-year-old who ate peanuts has hives. Which added findings mean anaphylaxis that calls for epinephrine? Select all that apply.
options: Wheezing and chest tightness
BP 78/50 with a weak pulse
Hoarse voice with stridor
Itching around the mouth
Hives spreading to the legs
Watery eyes and sneezing
explanation: Wheezing, hypotension and stridor show airway, breathing or circulatory involvement, which is anaphylaxis, so give epinephrine per local protocol. Spreading hives, itching or sneezing alone fit a simple allergic reaction.

stem: A 45-year-old diabetic man who took insulin and skipped lunch is confused, pale and sweaty with cool skin. Pulse 110, respirations 18. These findings best fit:
options: Hypoglycemia
Diabetic ketoacidosis
Hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state
Heat exhaustion
explanation: Rapid onset of confusion with cool, pale, diaphoretic skin after insulin without food is classic hypoglycemia; check the glucose. DKA develops over days with warm dry skin, fruity breath and deep rapid Kussmaul respirations.

stem: At a busy emergency department, you leave an unstable patient on a hallway stretcher without giving a report to staff. This is:
options: Battery
False imprisonment
Breach of confidentiality
Abandonment
explanation: Ending care without transferring it to someone of equal or higher training is abandonment. Battery is touching a patient without consent, which did not occur here.

stem: Four trauma patients have thigh injuries. Which one is an appropriate candidate for a traction splint?
options: Femur fracture with an unstable pelvis
Isolated closed midshaft femur fracture
Femur fracture with an ankle fracture on that leg
Fracture at the knee joint itself
explanation: A traction splint is for an isolated closed midshaft femur fracture. Pelvic, hip, knee or ankle injury on the same leg are contraindications because the splint anchors against or pulls through those structures.

stem: At a three-car crash at night, you find two injured drivers right away. Before committing to their care, you should:
options: Begin treating the louder of the two drivers
Walk the scene to account for every occupant
Ask the drivers whether anyone else was in their cars
Request air medical for both drivers
explanation: Size-up includes determining the total number of patients, and at night people may be thrown clear, wander off or be hidden in vehicles. Relying on injured drivers' reports can miss a patient.

stem: Palpating the chest of a 50-year-old crash victim, you feel crackling like crisped rice under the skin. This indicates:
options: Rib fragments grinding together
Air leaking into the soft tissue
Fluid collecting in both lower lung fields
Blood pooling under the skin
explanation: Crackling under the skin is subcutaneous emphysema from air leaking out of the lung or airway, a clue to pneumothorax. Grating of bone ends is felt at a fracture site, not as diffuse crackling under the skin.

stem: A 30-year-old man is found unresponsive with pinpoint pupils, shallow respirations of 4 per minute and SpO2 78%. Your first action should be:
options: Give naloxone before any other care
Apply a nonrebreather at 15 L/min
Place him in the recovery position
Ventilate with a BVM and oxygen
explanation: Inadequate breathing is the immediate life threat, so ventilate with a BVM first and then give naloxone per protocol. A nonrebreather does nothing for a patient who is barely breathing.

stem: A 26-year-old woman with epilepsy had a 2-minute generalized seizure. She is now drowsy and confused, breathing adequately with a clear airway. Her condition is best described as:
options: The postictal state
Status epilepticus
A brief absence seizure
A syncopal episode
explanation: Drowsiness and confusion that gradually improve after a seizure is the postictal phase; place her in the recovery position and monitor. Status epilepticus is a seizure lasting over 5 minutes or repeated seizures without regaining consciousness.

stem: A 70-year-old woman struck by a car has pelvic pain and instability on one gentle compression, pulse 120, and BP 88/60. You should:
options: Rock the pelvis again to confirm instability
Apply a pelvic binder at the greater trochanters
Apply a traction splint to the painful leg
Logroll her several times to inspect her back and buttocks
explanation: An unstable pelvis with shock signs calls for a pelvic binder centered over the greater trochanters to reduce pelvic volume and bleeding. Repeated rocking or logrolling can dislodge clots and worsen hemorrhage.

stem: A 26-year-old woman is alone in a crashed sedan, but an empty child safety seat is buckled in the back. You should:
options: Assume no child was in the car
Note the empty seat on the report and begin transport
Ask her about a child and search the area
Have police check her home later
explanation: An empty child seat is a classic clue to a possible hidden patient who may have been ejected or carried off by a bystander. Assuming the seat was empty can leave an injured child undiscovered.

stem: A 67-year-old man with prior heart attacks sits upright gasping, with crackles in both lungs, pink frothy sputum and ankle swelling. BP 170/100. The most likely cause is:
options: An acute asthma attack
Pulmonary edema from heart failure
A COPD exacerbation with bronchospasm
A spontaneous pneumothorax
explanation: Crackles, pink frothy sputum, edema and hypertension in a cardiac patient point to congestive heart failure with pulmonary edema, which may benefit from CPAP per protocol. Asthma and COPD typically produce wheezing rather than frothy sputum and crackles.

stem: An 84-year-old man is in cardiac arrest. His wife says he has a DNR order, but no one can find it. You should:
options: Begin resuscitation per local protocol
Withhold CPR based on her statement
Wait until she locates the form
Give compressions only, without ventilations
explanation: A DNR or POLST must be valid and present to withhold resuscitation, so start CPR and contact medical direction per local protocol. Withholding care on a verbal report alone is not supported.

stem: A 15-year-old asthmatic had loud wheezing 20 minutes ago. Now she is drowsy, breath sounds are barely audible, and SpO2 is 86%. This change most likely indicates:
options: The airway opening as she improves
Impending respiratory failure
Resolution after her inhaler
Anxiety-driven hyperventilation
explanation: A silent chest with falling mental status and SpO2 means too little air is moving to produce wheezes, so she is tiring toward respiratory arrest. Assist ventilations as needed and transport rapidly; quieter breath sounds here are not improvement.

stem: A 15-year-old skateboarder has a painful deformity of the left clavicle with good distal pulses and sensation. Which immobilization is most appropriate?
options: Traction splint
Sling and swathe
Long board splint along the arm
Air splint inflated to full pressure
explanation: A sling supports the arm and a swathe binds it to the chest, immobilizing the clavicle and shoulder. Traction and long rigid splints are for long-bone extremity fractures, not the shoulder girdle.

stem: A pickup rolled over in a field; its 30-year-old driver says three friends were riding in the bed, and you find one. You should:
options: Treat the driver and friend you have found
Request more units and search for the other two
Wait for the driver to recall where they landed
Assume the others left uninjured on foot
explanation: Occupants ejected from a truck bed may lie far from the vehicle and be critically injured, so the count must be reconciled and additional resources requested. Treating only the patients you see risks missing the sickest ones.

stem: An 81-year-old nursing home resident with a urinary catheter has new confusion, temperature 101.8 F, pulse 118, respirations 26 and BP 88/54. You should suspect:
options: Sepsis with shock
Progression of her dementia
Normal aging changes
A low blood sugar reaction
explanation: Fever, tachycardia, tachypnea, hypotension and new confusion with a catheter suggest sepsis, and confusion is often the main sign of infection in older adults. Never assume new confusion in an older patient is normal or due to dementia.

stem: A 70-year-old confused man takes metformin and insulin daily. This medication history should prompt you to:
options: Assist with his nitroglycerin
Withhold oxygen until ALS arrives
Check his blood glucose
Give oral glucose without testing
explanation: Insulin and metformin indicate diabetes, so altered mental status should prompt a glucose check. Oral glucose is given only when glucose is low and the patient can swallow and protect the airway.

stem: A 22-year-old motorcyclist in a full-face helmet is breathing adequately, the helmet fits snugly, and you have full airway access. You should:
options: Leave the helmet on and stabilize the head
Remove the helmet before applying a collar
Remove the helmet to look for scalp bleeding
Cut the chin strap and pull the helmet off
explanation: A well-fitting helmet that does not interfere with airway management or ventilation is left in place and stabilized. Remove it with two rescuers only if it blocks the airway, fits poorly or prevents CPR.

stem: A 22-year-old football player collapsed during practice in 95 F heat. He is confused and combative with hot skin, pulse 132 and BP 100/60. The life threat is:
options: Heat exhaustion
Heat cramps
Simple dehydration
Heat stroke
explanation: Altered mental status with high body temperature defines heat stroke, which needs aggressive cooling such as ice water immersion where possible and rapid transport. Heat exhaustion does not cause significant confusion, and exertional heat stroke patients may still be sweating.

stem: A 70-year-old man found outside on a 20 F night is confused with slurred speech. He has stopped shivering, and his pulse is 48. This indicates:
options: Moderate to severe hypothermia
Mild hypothermia
Normal response to cold
Alcohol intoxication without cold injury
explanation: Loss of shivering, altered mental status and bradycardia indicate moderate to severe hypothermia, so handle him gently to avoid triggering ventricular fibrillation. Mild hypothermia features vigorous shivering with an intact mental status.

stem: An unrestrained 34-year-old driver struck a tree. You note a starred windshield and a bent steering wheel. You should suspect:
options: Isolated knee and hip injuries from the dash
Only minor bruising since the airbag deployed
Head, neck, and chest injuries
An injury limited to the lower legs
explanation: A starred windshield suggests the head struck the glass, and a deformed steering wheel suggests chest impact, so head, cervical spine and chest injuries are likely. Airbag deployment does not exclude serious injury, especially in an unrestrained occupant.

stem: A 3-year-old has patterned burns and an inconsistent story. You report suspected abuse to child protective services. Under HIPAA, this report is:
options: Prohibited without the parents' written consent
Permitted, because state law requires it
Allowed only after the hospital reports first
Allowed only if police ask for it
explanation: HIPAA permits disclosures required by law, and EMTs are mandated reporters of suspected child abuse in most states. Waiting for parental consent would defeat the purpose of the report.

stem: A 61-year-old diabetic man is confused but follows commands and swallows normally. His glucose is 48 mg/dL. Per protocol, you should give:
options: Oral glucose only after he becomes unresponsive
Nothing by mouth until ALS arrives
Insulin from his own supply
Oral glucose, 15 to 25 g
explanation: Hypoglycemia with symptoms is treated with 15-25 g of oral glucose when the patient can swallow and protect the airway. An unresponsive patient must never receive anything by mouth, and insulin would worsen the low glucose.

stem: A 74-year-old man with hypertension reports sudden tearing pain in his lower back and abdomen. He is pale, BP 86/50, and you feel a pulsating abdominal mass. You should suspect:
options: A kidney stone
Lumbar muscle strain from lifting
Acute appendicitis
Abdominal aortic aneurysm
explanation: Sudden tearing abdominal or back pain, a pulsating mass and hypotension in an older hypertensive man suggest a leaking AAA; avoid palpating the mass further and transport rapidly. A kidney stone causes severe flank pain but not a pulsating mass or shock.

stem: A 28-year-old woman with a missed period has sudden sharp lower left abdominal pain and dizziness. She is pale, pulse 124, BP 92/60. The most likely life threat is:
options: Urinary tract infection
Ordinary menstrual cramps with nausea
Food poisoning
Ruptured ectopic pregnancy
explanation: Any woman of childbearing age with abdominal pain, a missed period and signs of shock should be treated as a ruptured ectopic pregnancy with internal bleeding. Treat for shock and transport rapidly; benign causes do not produce tachycardia and hypotension.

stem: Called for an unresponsive 19-year-old in a dorm room, you see a syringe and a bent spoon on the desk. These clues suggest:
options: Possible opioid overdose and a sharps hazard
A diabetic patient who injected too much of his insulin
A seizure disorder with a missed medication
A head injury from a fall out of bed
explanation: The environment gives the nature of illness: a spoon and syringe point to injected drugs such as opioids and warn of uncapped needles. Insulin users do not need a spoon, and the scene does not suggest trauma.

stem: An 8-year-old girl weighing 25 kg has hives, wheezing, and lip swelling after eating peanuts. Which epinephrine auto-injector dose and site?
options: 0.3 mg in the deltoid
0.15 mg in the deltoid
0.15 mg in the anterolateral thigh
0.5 mg in the anterolateral thigh muscle
explanation: Children weighing 15-30 kg receive the 0.15 mg auto-injector, and adults or patients over 30 kg receive 0.3 mg, both injected into the anterolateral thigh. The deltoid is not the recommended site for auto-injectors.

stem: While assessing a 40-year-old man during a behavioral emergency, which finding most strongly warns that he may become violent?
options: Quiet crying while seated
Clenched fists and pacing toward you
Slow speech with a flat affect
Repeated questions about the hospital
explanation: Clenched fists, pacing, a loud voice and moving toward the crew are warning signs of imminent violence, so keep an exit open and request law enforcement. Crying or a flat affect suggests sadness or depression rather than aggression.

stem: A 66-year-old woman fell and struck her head. She takes warfarin daily. This history matters because she:
options: Has a higher risk of brain bleeding
Should get aspirin before transport
Can be released if her exam is normal
Most likely had a seizure first
explanation: Anticoagulants such as warfarin raise the risk of intracranial bleeding after even minor head trauma, so she needs transport and close reassessment. A normal initial exam does not rule out a slow bleed.

stem: A 25-year-old man was shot in the abdomen at an active crime scene secured by police. When exposing the wound, you should:
options: Wait for police photos before exposing it
Cut straight through the hole for speed
Cut around the bullet hole, not through it
Remove all clothing and leave it on the ground
explanation: Patient care comes first, but cutting around holes and bagging clothing preserves evidence. Delaying care for police photos is wrong because treatment takes priority.

stem: A 4-year-old sits leaning forward and drooling, with a fever of 103 F, a muffled voice and soft stridor that began suddenly. These findings most suggest:
options: Croup
Bronchiolitis
Epiglottitis
Simple ear infection
explanation: Sudden high fever, drooling, tripod positioning and a muffled voice suggest epiglottitis; keep the child calm with the parent and never examine the throat. Croup develops gradually with a barking cough and low-grade fever.

stem: At a mass-casualty incident using START, assign each adult patient a category.
rows: Cannot walk, RR 20, radial pulse, obeys
Cannot walk, RR 22, no radial pulse
Cannot walk, RR 18, cannot obey commands
explanation: Walking patients are minor, and anyone who cannot walk is immediate with respirations over 30, no radial pulse or failure to obey commands. Only the patient who passes all three checks is delayed, even though he cannot walk.

stem: A 19-year-old with asthma is wheezing and has his prescribed albuterol inhaler with a spacer. After checking the medication, which instruction is correct?
options: Inhale quickly, then exhale right after the puff
Spray it into the mouth while exhaling
Exhale fully, then inhale deeply as it is activated
Take four rapid puffs without pausing
explanation: Shake the inhaler, have the patient exhale fully, seal the lips around the spacer, and press the canister while he inhales slowly and deeply, then hold the breath about 10 seconds. Spraying during exhalation or rapid repeated puffs deposits little drug in the lungs.

stem: For each finding, specify whether it points to tension pneumothorax, cardiac tamponade, or both.
rows: Absent breath sounds on one side
explanation: Absent breath sounds on one side and a late tracheal shift point to tension pneumothorax, and muffled heart sounds to tamponade. Both block blood return to the heart, so distended neck veins and hypotension do not tell them apart.

stem: A 55-year-old driver struck the steering wheel. A section of his left chest moves inward when he inhales and outward when he exhales. This finding indicates:
options: A single rib fracture
Cardiac tamponade
An open pneumothorax
Flail chest
explanation: Paradoxical movement of a chest wall segment means two or more adjacent ribs are broken in two or more places; support ventilation with a BVM if breathing is inadequate. A single rib fracture causes pain but not paradoxical motion.

stem: A 26-year-old man is unresponsive with pinpoint pupils, cyanosis, SpO2 78%, and respirations of 4 per minute. Your first action should be:
options: Give 4 mg naloxone intranasally
Ventilate with a BVM and oxygen
Apply a nonrebreather at 15 L/min
Perform a sternal rub to arouse him
explanation: Ventilation comes first because hypoxia kills before naloxone (0.4 mg IM/IN or 4 mg IN per protocol) takes effect. A nonrebreather cannot help a patient breathing 4 times a minute.

stem: A 55-year-old man with an open leg fracture cannot walk, breathes 20 per minute, has a radial pulse, and obeys commands. Using START, tag him:
options: Immediate (red)
Minor (green)
Delayed (yellow)
Expectant (black)
explanation: He fails only the walking test: respirations under 30, radial pulse present and following commands make him delayed. The painful fracture does not by itself make him immediate under START.

stem: A 27-year-old with a stab wound just left of the sternum has distended neck veins, muffled heart sounds, equal breath sounds and BP 80/66. These signs suggest:
options: Tension pneumothorax
Cardiac tamponade
An open pneumothorax
Neurogenic shock
explanation: JVD, muffled heart tones and hypotension with a narrow pulse pressure form Beck's triad of cardiac tamponade, which needs rapid transport for surgical care. Equal breath sounds make tension pneumothorax less likely.

stem: While restraining a combative patient, a used needle punctures your gloved hand. After washing the site, you should:
options: Report it promptly to the infection control officer
Wait to see whether symptoms develop
Ask the patient yourself for an HIV test
Report it to your supervisor at the start of next shift
explanation: Exposures should be washed and reported immediately to the designated infection control officer, because post-exposure treatment works best within hours. Waiting for symptoms or the next shift delays that care.

stem: A 45-year-old who fell from a ladder now responds only to pain. Which findings make up Cushing's triad of rising intracranial pressure? (Choose three.)
options: Slowing pulse rate
Falling blood pressure
Irregular respirations
Pinpoint pupils
Rising blood pressure
Rapid, weak pulse
explanation: Rising blood pressure, a slowing pulse and irregular respirations form Cushing's triad, a late sign of brain herniation that needs rapid transport. A rapid weak pulse with falling pressure is the opposite pattern, hypovolemic shock.

stem: By radio, medical direction orders nitroglycerin 0.4 mg sublingual for your 63-year-old chest pain patient. Before giving it, you should:
options: Give it immediately to save transport time
Repeat the order back, then check the rights
Wait until handoff to confirm the order
Ask the patient if the dose sounds right
explanation: Repeating the order word for word catches errors, then verify the rights: right patient, medication, dose, route, time and documentation, plus the expiration date. Giving it without confirmation risks a dose or drug error.

stem: Place the parts of the patient assessment for a responsive medical patient in the order they are performed.
options: Secondary assessment
Scene size-up
Reassessment en route
History taking
Primary assessment
explanation: Scene safety comes first, then life threats in the primary assessment; a responsive medical patient's history guides the secondary exam, and reassessment continues to handoff. In an unresponsive patient the rapid exam comes before the history from bystanders.

stem: A 38-year-old driver in a side-impact crash has left upper abdominal tenderness and left shoulder pain. Pulse 122, BP 102/78, skin pale and cool. You should suspect:
options: A rotator cuff tear
A seat belt abrasion
A bruised rib from the intruding door panel
Splenic injury with internal bleeding
explanation: Left upper quadrant tenderness with referred left shoulder pain and signs of compensated shock suggest a bleeding spleen. Treat for shock and transport rapidly; attributing the tachycardia to pain or a minor injury delays care.

stem: Place the START triage checks in the order you perform them.
options: Check radial pulse or capillary refill
Direct walking patients to one area
Check ability to follow commands
Assess breathing and respiratory rate
explanation: START moves the walking wounded first, then checks respirations, perfusion and mental status (RPM) in that order. Breathing is checked before perfusion because an airway or rate problem kills fastest.

stem: A 3-year-old ate an unknown number of her grandmother's pills 30 minutes ago and is alert. Regarding activated charcoal, you should:
options: Give it right away for every pill ingestion
Induce vomiting first, then give it
Give it only if medical direction orders it
Mix it with milk before giving it
explanation: Contact Poison Control or medical direction; activated charcoal is given only on their order and never to a patient who cannot swallow or protect the airway. Inducing vomiting is not recommended, and milk reduces charcoal's binding.

stem: A 60-year-old pedestrian struck by a car has pelvic pain and instability with one gentle compression. Pulse 128, BP 90/60. Your main concern is:
options: Severe internal bleeding from the pelvis
Bladder rupture causing later abdominal infection
Hip dislocation
Nerve damage to the legs
explanation: An unstable pelvic fracture can hide a large volume of blood loss, so apply a pelvic binder per protocol, treat for shock and transport rapidly. Do not rock or repeatedly compress the pelvis, which can worsen bleeding.

stem: You and your partner lift a 90 kg patient on a cot. Using the power lift technique, you should:
options: Bend at the waist and lift with your back
Twist your torso to turn as you lift
Lock your back and lift with your legs
Hold the cot well away from your body
explanation: The power lift keeps the back locked, feet shoulder-width apart, the load close, and the legs doing the work. Twisting or lifting with the back is a common cause of EMS back injury.

stem: A 24-year-old has a gunshot wound to the right chest that bubbles and makes a sucking sound with each breath. Your immediate priority is:
options: Pack the wound tightly with gauze
Seal it with an occlusive dressing
Cover it with a bulky dry dressing
Roll him onto his uninjured side to breathe
explanation: An open chest wound lets air enter the pleural space, so seal it immediately with an occlusive dressing and watch for tension pneumothorax, burping the dressing if needed. A dry gauze dressing lets air pass through.

stem: At a school bus crash, a 4-year-old is not breathing after you open the airway but has a palpable pulse. Under JumpSTART you should:
options: Give 5 rescue breaths and reassess
Tag her expectant and move on
Begin chest compressions immediately
Tag her delayed until more help arrives
explanation: JumpSTART recognizes that apnea in children is often respiratory, so an apneic child with a pulse gets 5 rescue breaths; if breathing resumes she is immediate. Tagging her expectant without the breaths, as in adult START, would miss a salvageable child.

stem: During delivery of a full-term infant, the head delivers and you feel the umbilical cord wrapped loosely around the neck. You should:
options: Clamp and cut the cord immediately
Gently slip the cord over the head
Pull the infant out quickly to ease tension
Push the head back into the vagina
explanation: A loose nuchal cord is slipped over the head; only if it is too tight to move is it clamped in two places and cut between per protocol. Pulling on the infant can tear the cord or injure the baby.
